name: Trolamine salicylate
lead: Trolamine salicylate (triethanolamine salicylate) is a salt of triethanolamine and salicylic acid with two roles that touch appearance. In sunscreens and cosmetics it has served as a UVB-absorbing ingredient, and sun protection is the main way skin avoids the sunburn, uneven pigment and photoaging that change how a face looks over the years.[1][11] In over-the-counter creams such as Aspercreme it is used as an odourless rub for sore muscles and joints, and people who train hard use such rubs to ease soreness between sessions, which is the chain by which it connects to building and keeping a physique.[1][2][8]

The salicylate part absorbs UVB, the triethanolamine neutralises its acidity, and the compound has no smell, unlike menthol-based rubs.[1] Products are marketed for temporary relief of minor aches in muscles and joints from arthritis, backache, strains and sprains.[1][2] In 2019 the US FDA proposed classifying its use in sunscreens as not generally recognised as safe and effective.[1][11]

Human trials of the cream date from the 1980s and 1990s and examined knee osteoarthritis and exercise-induced muscle soreness, with differing results across studies. Absorption studies in animals and people show that salicylate from the topical salt enters the skin and reaches underlying tissue.[4][5][6][7]

paras: Trolamine salicylate has been listed as a UVB filter, absorbing in the 290 to 315 nm band that causes sunburn.[1] Organic filters of this type take in ultraviolet light and release the energy as heat or lower-energy radiation, a mechanism distinct from the mineral filters zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.[11] Reviews of sunscreen regulation describe how the FDA has sorted older filters into safety categories, and as of 2021 only the two mineral filters were classed as generally recognised as safe and effective in the US.[11][12] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, says use of the salt in sunscreens has been discontinued.[3]

For appearance, the reason to use any broad-spectrum filter is long-term: Wikipedia's sunscreen article summarises studies in which regular daily sunscreen use was associated with smoother, more resilient skin over several years, and notes that the evidence on wrinkles and sagging is limited.[11] Trolamine salicylate was a weak, UVB-only contributor to such products, and the sunscreen article states that it was reclassified as not generally recognised as safe and effective.[1][11]

US label wording for a trolamine salicylate product states it is for temporary relief of minor aches and pains of muscles and joints associated with arthritis, simple backache, lumbago, neuralgia, strains, bruises and sprains, for external use only.[2] Wikipedia notes that listed products are 10% solutions.[1] Brands include Aspercreme, Aspergel, Mobisyl, Myoflex and Sportscreme.[1][3]

In gym and sports settings these creams are discussed as a way to ease muscle soreness. A 2001 T Nation member asked which sports cream worked best for sore muscles and whether they all needed trolamine salicylate as the main ingredient.[13] A delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) conference abstract cited by Wikipedia reported that users of the 10% cream described later onset, less intense and shorter soreness than placebo users, and that the chemical was found in muscle tissue.[1]

As a salicylate it is described as inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes and so reducing prostaglandin production locally.[3] A 1984 pig study found that at least 82% of an applied dose was absorbed over two hours, with salicylate localising in underlying skeletal muscle.[4] A 1996 randomised human crossover study compared serum salicylate after topical methyl salicylate and trolamine salicylate application, finding measurable systemic salicylate after topical use of these derivatives.[5] A 2019 pharmaceutics paper designed and evaluated a film-forming system for topical delivery of the compound.[15]
Wikipedia states that the FDA has not reviewed the listed OTC products and that manufacturers have not given the agency evidence of absorption into underlying tissue.[1]

The compound is a 1:1 salt of the tertiary amine triethanolamine and salicylic acid with the formula C13H21NO6 and a molar mass of about 287.3 g/mol.[1] Grokipedia describes it as a pale to amber liquid or solid that dissolves readily in water and alcohols, made by neutralising salicylic acid with triethanolamine.[3]

Wikipedia lists a GHS warning for serious eye damage, skin and eye irritation, and harm if swallowed.[1] Labels advise external use only, and Grokipedia says use should be avoided on broken skin and under occlusive dressings.[2][3]

Because salicylates are related to aspirin, product labelling for topical salicylate products generally carries external-use-only wording and advice to stop use if irritation develops.[2] The review of sunscreen regulation and safety in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology covers the FDA's category system and the ingredients for which safety data were judged insufficient.[12]

A 1982 JAMA report examined a trolamine salicylate cream in knee osteoarthritis, with a related letter published the same year, and a later study examined a single topical application of a 10% cream in osteoarthritis symptoms.[6][14][7] Studies of delayed-onset muscle soreness include a 1991 randomised trial of ultrasound with trolamine salicylate phonophoresis in 40 young women and a 1989 trial of a 10% cream after a reproducible weight-training programme.[8][9] A 1988 conference abstract cited by Wikipedia reported less soreness with the product than placebo.[1] A 1999 rat study compared topical agents including trolamine salicylate for failing skin flaps.[10] No clinical trials of its sunscreen performance were found.

The FDA's 2019 proposal moved trolamine salicylate, with other older organic filters, away from sunscreen status; the FDA's categorisation process assessed older filters against current safety-data expectations.[1][12] Wikipedia's sunscreen article states that the compound is listed among filters not generally recognised as safe and effective in the US, and gives the year as 2021 when the final classification was reached.[11] Sold as a muscle rub the product remains an over-the-counter item in the US under external analgesic labelling.[2]

timeline.event: JAMA publishes a trial of trolamine salicylate cream in knee osteoarthritis.[6]
A pig study reports absorption and localisation of salicylate in skeletal muscle after topical application.[4]
A trial of a 10% cream is reported in weight-training-induced muscle soreness.[9]
A human crossover study compares serum salicylate after topical salicylate derivatives.[5]
The US FDA proposes that trolamine salicylate in sunscreens is not generally recognised as safe and effective.[1]

card.summary: A weak salicylate UVB filter better known as the active in odourless muscle-pain creams.
card.note: FDA proposed in 2019 that its sunscreen use is not generally recognised as safe and effective.

quick.overview:
Trolamine salicylate is a salicylate salt best known as the active ingredient in over-the-counter topical pain creams. It has also been used as a weak UVB sunscreen filter.

In 2019 the US FDA proposed that its sunscreen use is not generally recognised as safe and effective.
quick.mechanism: The salicylate part absorbs UVB and is described as inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes locally; triethanolamine neutralises the acid.
quick.risks: Labels say external use only. Listed hazards include eye damage and skin or eye irritation. Absorbed salicylate has been measured in blood after topical use in a small human study.

chain: Absorbs UVB in a sunscreen or cosmetic base; or is rubbed on sore muscles
Less sun-related skin damage; or less perceived soreness
Skin that holds up better over the years; or more comfortable training
angle.text: In sunscreens trolamine salicylate acted as a weak UVB filter, one of the ingredients formulators have used to protect skin from burning and photoaging. As a muscle rub it is used for post-workout soreness so that a person can keep training.
